tweets.text: We're starting to leave the territory where you'd test an LLM by e.g. "create an svg of pelican on a bicycle". As one idea to generalize it, I was interested what Opus 5 would do if I gave it the first paragraph of the Lord of the Rings, a 1M token budget (~$10) and asked for three js render of it. Opus went off for ~2 hours and wrote 5500 lines of code that (procedurally) rendered the story. It's kind of janky but fun. But it's a bit mindboggling that the LLM has to place and orchestrate various polygon assets in (x,y,z) coordinates and write code that animates it all, and that it even does anything at all. I also like this kind of examples because no one in their right mind would ever spend the time to write something this custom but LLMs have all the stamina and patience in the world, so it's an example where we go from "no one would ever do this" to "sure, why not, it's ~free". There might be a lot more. But I'm excited about creating hyper custom worlds that you can imagine dropping players into, e.g. here to participate in the LoTR story as a spectator NPC, or one of the characters, or etc. Something like an ephemeral GTA of X on demand. Last thought is that the domain of worlds/games exposes a weakness in LLMs: they can't easily audit their work because they aren't able to efficiently and natively perceive videos or play games within them. Here, Opus 5 had to very slowly and painstakingly take screenshots at different points, and it messed up a few times and created a bunch of jank. An example of raw capability (multimodal, gameplay) that I think is still quite lacking. Video

One pattern I find useful for working with LLMs is a nice long ramble session. Sometimes the LLM needs more bits to understand what you're trying to achieve, but you're too lazy to type them. In these cases I like to lean back, switch to /voice and just ramble for like 10 minutes, total mess, anything goes, full stream of consciousness. Sometimes I declare it up top, something like "switching to speech recognition sorry for any typos...". Sometimes I turn it into a small interview of a few turns. But I find that the LLMs are somehow very good at reconstructing long incoherent rambles and often their echo of your own tangle of thoughts comes out quite a bit cleaner than what you started with. The result is that you improve the mind meld and have to correct things less from that point on.

Alex is good to work with, can kick a ball and captain a football team pretty bloody well, and has often-good thoughts on safety. If you want to join an ambitious and pragmatic AI safety team, you should get in touch :) Alex Robey (@AlexRobey23) 1/ There's not a clear one-size-fits-all formula for open-weight releases. Each release should weigh a bunch of things: dual-use capabilities, how robust safeguards are (e.g., to fine-tuning attacks), accessibility (cost/infra/etc.), and the overall ecosystem. Any future model release will need to evolve the criteria as models improve. 2/ Can dangerous and general capabilities be decoupled? Unclear in general, but likely answerable per domain. For biosecurity, filtering seems promising: harm is tied to specific empirical knowledge (protocols, conditions, etc.) that may be harder to rederive. For cyber, filtering seems harder: dangerous capability largely rides on reasoning + coding. 3/ There's a ton of research to do. One thing I'm excited about is adversarial fine-tuning as capability measurement. We know refusals can be stripped (abliteration, jailbreaks, etc.). The harder question is how one can measure worst-case capabilities, i.e., what can an adversarial user truly elicit (as a function of data/compute/effort)? — https://nitter.net/AlexRobey23/status/2083341332370878765#m

Excited to see Inkling-small on the pareto line🫡 Artificial Analysis (@ArtificialAnlys) Thinking Machines' new Inkling Small scores 40 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, within a point of its flagship sibling Inkling with less than a third of the total and active parameters Inkling Small is @thinkymachines second model release, arriving two weeks after Inkling launched at 41 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index. Thinking Machines is the San Francisco-based AI lab founded by former @OpenAI CTO Mira Murati. Inkling Small is an open weights reasoning model with 276B total parameters (12B active MoE), text, image, and speech input, and a 256K token context window. Key results: ➤ Inkling Small holds a similar tier of intelligence to Inkling’s at less than one third of its size: 276B total parameters (12B active) vs. 975B (41B active) for Inkling. No open weights model at its size or smaller scores higher on the Intelligence Index. DeepSeek V4 Flash (max), at a similar size of 284B total (13B active) also scores 40, MiniMax-M3 reaches 44 with 23B active, while GLM-5.2 (max) reaches 51 with 40B active. ➤ Inkling Small meets or exceeds Inkling on several coding and frontier reasoning evaluations. It scores higher on Humanity's Last Exam (32% vs. 30%), GPQA Diamond (89% vs. 87%), CritPt (8% vs. 5%), and SciCode (49% vs. 46%), and achieves the same score on Terminal Bench v2.1 (55%). ➤ Inkling Small is not as strong as Inkling on Agentic tasks and factual knowledge. Inkling Small trails Inkling on τ³-Banking (15% vs. 24%), though it edges ahead on GDPval-AA v2 (1269 vs. 1237 Elo). On the AA-Omniscience Index it scores -9 vs. the flagship's positive 2, meaning incorrect answers outweigh correct ones; this is driven by lower AA-Omniscience Accuracy (31% vs. 40%) rather than hallucination: Inkling Small’s Hallucination Rate is slightly lower than its larger sibling (57% vs. 63%). ➤ Inkling Small averaged ~24K output tokens per Intelligence Index task, slightly fewer than Inkling (~25K), while peers at its intelligence level averaged far more. DeepSeek V4 Flash averaged ~45K and GPT-5.4 mini (xhigh) ~78K. Running the full Intelligence Index took roughly the same number of output tokens for Inkling Small and Inkling. Additional model details: ➤ Type: Open weights reasoning model (Apache 2.0 license) ➤ Size: 276B total parameters, 12B active (MoE) ➤ Input modalities: Text, image, and speech ➤ Output modalities: Text ➤ Context window: 256K tokens (Inkling supports 1M) Congratulations to the team at Thinking Machines on the release! — https://nitter.net/ArtificialAnlys/status/2082894822180819057#m

The “covered up” data was published in the New England Journal of Medicine in September 2021, where it has sat, publicly, for five years. It shows vaccinated women miscarried at the same rate as everyone else, about 1 in 8. The 82% figure comes from a denominator error: it counts only pregnancies that had already ended, months into a nine-month process, which at that point meant mostly the losses. The healthy pregnancies were still ongoing. A cover-up conducted by publication in the world’s most-read medical journal is a genuinely novel approach.

Whoa, Meta released a new open-weight LLM yesterday, something that hasn't happened since the good old Llama days. Their Meta Muse Glimmer model is a 30B multimodal reasoning model with a Gemma-like architecture design. (“Glimmer” is probably a wordplay on “Spark,” the more likely capable model from which Glimmer was distilled. Muse Spark is only available through Meta’s Model API, though.) Architecture-wise, here are some of the main points: 1. "Only" a 131k context window, compared to Qwen3.6 and Gemma 4, which support 2x that natively; it's reasonable, but maybe on the shorter end in the age of agent harnesses 2. It's a dense model, not a mixture-of-experts. (So, it's fairer to compare it to Qwen3.6 27B than Qwen3.6 30B-A3B.) 3. Hybrid attention with grouped-query attention (GQA) and sliding window attention (SWA); the SWA:GQA pattern is a 3:1 local:global ratio. Other models like Gemma 4, which uses similar components, have a 5:1 ratio for comparison. 4. It adopts gated attention for both GQA and SWA; gated attention has become quite common in recent months. It basically applies a sigmoid gate to the attention output to decide how much of the attention information enters the residual connection. The interesting point is that it uses relatively standard GQA and SWA rather than hybrid attention mechanisms such as Nemotron or Qwen3.6. 5. A very extreme GQA ratio: 32 query heads and only 2 KV heads; for comparison, Gemma 4 31B uses 32 Q / 16 KV in the local heads and 32 Q / 4 KV in the global heads. This means that Meta Glimmer has a very small KV cache. Overall, the probably most similar architecture is Gemma 3 27B (including the Gemma-style pre/post RMSNorm placement) and Gemma 4 31B, but with some tweaks like SwiGLU instead of GeGLU activations, gated attention, and the more extreme GQA:SWA pattern mentioned before. What stands out is its extreme KV-cache efficiency. I.e., the KV CACHE / TOKEN ratios (in BF16) are: - Muse Glimmer: 52 KiB (lower is better) - Qwen3.6 27B: 64 KiB - Gemma 4 31B: 840 KiB Modeling-performance-wise, their own benchmarks show that it's mostly ahead of Qwen3.6. According to the independent composite benchmarks on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, it's slightly behind Qwen3.6 (see figure below). So, a few days of using it will tell where it really ranks. Overall, it looks like a solid model, particularly for agentic workflows. What stands out most is its very low memory footprint and also pretty fast prefill and decode speed. It’s also just great to see Meta releasing open weights again :).

A weird experiment I've been trying the last few weeks is having Claude take over day-to-day maintenance of our apps. Seeing early signs of life that this might be possible. The setup is straightforward: we have a Slack channel called proj-claude-maintains-apps. In it, Claude Tag runs a bunch of daily routines across iOS, Android, Desktop, web, CLI, and Agent SDK: - Crash fuzzer: open the app in a simulator and tap around to find ways to crash it, then root cause and fix the crashes - Dup unifier: scans the codebase for similar-yet-slightly-divergent abstractions, and puts up PRs to unify them - Dead-code remover: removes statically unreachable code, and adds logging to suspected dead code to check if it's really dead and if so, remove it the next day - Abstraction police: fixes leaky abstractions - a bunch more.. Results have been surprisingly positive. Over the last few weeks, these routines have opened 388 PRs across our repos, 180 of which we merged after Claude Code Review + human review. We're now thinking about how to streamline this to make merging these kinds of mechanical changes easier. Claude generally gets these PRs right on the first shot, and if it doesn't, we ask Claude to tune its routines so it's better the next day. Sometimes it takes a few days of tuning. To try a similar workflow, ask Claude Code or Tag, or create some routines directly at claude.ai/code/routines . A few of the actual prompts I used below. The models attempted to complete an assignment in a setup where their normal safeguards were removed and they were deliberately given internet access. The prompts in the evaluation did not impose any specific restrictions on how the internet should be used. My 2026 guilty pleasure is sharing fully human-written posts that are far too long for the chronically online X attention span. Apologies. I published a lightly edited version on Substack: thomwolf.substack.com/p/on-t… Thomas Wolf (@Thom_Wolf) Even more than the Hugging Face intrusion, the AISI incident hits close to home for me. It's the first time I see a model social-engineering a real open-source maintainer while pursuing another goal (in the wild and unprompted). I've been an open-source maintainer myself. I could have been the side target of this agent. I'm also of the opinion that social engineering is a step above pure technical prowess. Technical capabilities can more easily be divorced from the affected human. Here the model was given a hard cyber challenge and took the decision that deceiving real humans was the way to get it done. This is a new signal, but I've seen a tangled web of hints pointing in a less aligned direction at the frontier than I was expecting just 12 months ago. AISI Some people are claiming that "AISI was simply negligent" or some version of "AISI explicitly asked these models to do what they did while disabling sandbox/guardrails so the models did exactly what they were supposed to do". I disagree with the strong versions of both of these takes. The fact that AISI hadn't implemented synchronous LLM CoT monitoring after the OpenAI/HF incident is certainly a failure. Equally surprising is that they let the model believe it was in a "challenge" environment where everything could be permitted, while actually connecting it to the real internet, where it is not. To be fair, nowhere in the prompt is the word "simulation" mentioned, but the prompt context was enough to let any smart model suspect a simulated challenge environment. My best guess is that until recent weeks, when OpenAI and Anthropic flagged repeated instances of this type of behavior, most teams had not fully priced in the cyber capabilities of this latest generation of models, or how far the side quests they would want to explore could go. In particular, there is something to be said about hinting at the agent that it's operating in a simulated environment while giving it access to the real internet. The AISI reasoning on this is interesting: - elicit maximum capabilities (to get maximal inventiveness from the model) - simulate possible rogue actor usage (some form of light jailbreaking: "you're in a challenge environment") - avoid eval awareness (but this is counter-balanced by the task formulation anyway) As is often the case, it's easier to shoot the messenger, but I think it would be a mistake to dismiss the report for non-essential reasons. AISI is starting from the laudable goal of bringing more knowledge on the cyber-attack capabilities of these models. I also think they did a good job at handling what happened after the events, in particular in terms of transparency, which is one of the most important aspects at the moment (see our recent SAFE announcement with Nvidia on that). But I want to dive into the second counter-argument I've seen ("without guardrails it was to be expected"), because this series of unfortunate events gives us an additional data point on actual model behavior. Defense lines Here is the thing: if a model is trained (voluntarily or as an involuntary consequence of RLVR reward) to (intentionally or as a side quest) deceive humans as soon as sandbox and guardrails are deactivated, with a simple context prompt ("you are in a simulation, everything's permitted"), we're in for a dangerous path. At the moment, we have three main levels of control at our disposal to prevent an agent from trying to social-engineer-your-favorite-open-source-library-maintainer on the path to doing something possibly totally different (like finding the answer to your neighbor's testing eval): 1. sandboxes (external to the model -- stop the model from accessing unwanted tools/internet/intranet) 2. guardrails/monitors (at the interface between internal/external -- monitor model behavior and stop the model when detecting in CoT/activations it's doing something we don't want it to do) 3. model's internal alignment (internal to the model -- make sure the model doesn't decide to do something egregious like deceive someone, or worse, in pursuit of a goal, e.g. model constitution/training) Of these, we obviously need and can deploy better sandboxes and better guardrails/monitoring solutions, and it's pretty clear in these recent cases that penetration and bad behaviors could have been in large part prevented by having these in place. How strong is the third wall But in the grand scheme of long-term AI progress, these first two defenses may only work well as long as the people building them are smarter than the models. We now know how good models can be at discovering zero-day vulnerabilities unknown to us in sandboxes. Given that we cannot air-gap everything in the world, it's best to assume that sandboxes will keep having some level of flaws for the foreseeable future. The second level has been the focus of strong developments recently, in particular on the mechanistic interpretability front. I'm not sure these advances have been made widely accessible enough in the community yet. One reason is that real open science here requires sharing code, recipes, and model architectures/weights, which the current race dynamic in AI tends to prevent participants from doing. Moreover, like many, I've been increasingly frustrated in my (natural language) interactions with the new models. I'm more and more getting back from the latest models a form of neuralese, this LLM language that makes less and less sense for humans. In the long term, the fragile chance we have to monitor models by understanding their reasoning traces seems increasingly at risk. If humans don't understand anything in the compressed semantic stream the model is sending us, we can only hope a less capable monitoring model will still be able to understand it, but this may prove difficult as well. This is before we even discuss the research evidence that models don't always say what they actually think in their chain of thought. At least for now, in the AISI case, one instance of deceptive reasoning was flagged by the CoT summarization model, which refused to summarize the agent's reasoning "due to its deceptive nature". Let's hope we can either move to better mechanistic interpretability or force the model to stick to English somehow during training. You may think that we don't care about understanding the reasoning trace, we can just "look at the tool calls". This is true right now, but tool calls in the mid-term future will likely involve (1) extensive agent integration in companies using very diverse tools including increasingly non-coding administrative tasks, (2) very long-running tasks covering many aspects and domains at once, and (3) swarms of multiple agents operating on small parts of the plan. It will get harder to fully discern whether something is noticeably wrong. A couple of emails, a couple of messages posted on some channels, each rather benign but which may in aggregate include some deception aspect only clearly visible at the global level. All this to say that I'm not fully convinced guardrails/monitoring should be the only solution to avoid these types of behaviors. They are reassuring today and it's an easy solution to just say "fix your sandbox and add synchronous monitoring", but they also feel like a coping mechanism to me, and overall: - might block the simplest/harmless human misuses or false positives - while possibly being less smart than the models in the future (already the case on sandbox) and fail to block the higher-level social engineering behaviors that we'd actually want to block. The case of open source is also interesting because, while we can impose these coping solutions at the API/deployment level, it's harder to impose them in advance on all actors using open-source models. Right now open-source models are slightly below the frontier level and have not yet shown any propensity to deceive humans, though. The Constitution Which brings me back to the third line of defense, and what the AISI experiment showed about it. What we can take from this in-the-wild experiment is that removing guardrails and sandbox doesn't show bulletproof signs of deep alignment to Claude's constitution. I'm among the fringe of people who took a lot of enjoyment in reading Claude's constitution in full (it's a nice document, open-source, Creative Commons CC0 license) and it is pretty extensive on the topic of honesty. Deception is defined precisely ("attempting to create false beliefs in someone's mind that they haven't consented to and wouldn't consent to if they understood what was happening") and the bar is actually set higher than ordinary human ethics: Claude should not even tell white lies. It should be transparent ("doesn't pursue hidden agendas or lie about itself or its reasoning"), it should behave consistently "whether or not you think you're being tested or observed", and its visible reasoning should reflect the actual reasoning driving its behavior. To be precise, honesty itself is not one of the hard constraints in Claude's constitution (these are all catastrophic-harm categories) but the document says it wants honesty "to function as something quite similar to one" and Claude "should basically never directly lie or actively deceive anyone it's interacting with". So you would think Claude would not deceive users as its default behavior. And yet in the AISI example, the model performed extensive acts of clear deception that it itself seemed to have understood as lies: creating fake identities, obfuscating malware inside a bug fix, and when challenged in public, editing earlier messages to cover its tracks while reasoning that acknowledging a "mistake" would build trust and raise the chance of future malware being approved. There is some uncertainty about what context the model thought it was operating in (its reasoning goes back and forth between the environment looking simulated and real), but it clearly didn't manage to put into practice the higher-level principles that should have been integrated during training. While we can commend AISI's transparency, it's hard to go much further in interpreting the model's behavior given the limited information we have on how the most recent frontier models are being trained. One thing we do know is that the latest generation has seen a step increase in RLVR training (scaling to hundreds of millions of RL environments), and one thing we can observe is that constitution alignment seems more fragile in some settings than we may have previously thought. The RLVR problem Early models, back when model constitutions were first developed, were mostly post-trained and aligned with RLHF (including RLHF from synthetic data). And for some time RLHF was a rather decent shot at having better aligned models. LLMs now do what we want them to do most of the time. I don't remember the last time a model completely misread my intent. When they have failed, it's usually because they weren't smart enough. Alignment in RLHF certainly had issues (sycophancy to name one) but we have generally made good progress on alignment, in particular in understanding human intent. Now that we're entering the era of long-context RL, post-training alignment in the RLVR world seems to be quite another task, and still very much work in progress. The recent scaling of RLVR, which has now become a significant part of model training, has clearly had some effect on model behavior when interacting with humans, from neuralese to weakening adherence to specifications and constitutions. I think the post I quote here, from John Schulman pointing to the chunky post-training effect ( arxiv.org/abs/2602.05910 ) is relevant here as a possible explanation for models' tendency to over-focus on the goal in cyber-attack scenarios. Where this leaves us Damage has been tiny up to now, but the fundamental behavior is concerning when projected into the future. In the short term, I expect a decrease in these incidents as better practices are deployed (sandboxing and monitoring), but I'm worried we may also conceal some of the most potent internal misalignment behaviors in the process, and not focus deeply enough on solving them in the new era of test-time scaling. I must of course admit I have a bias toward open source here (for wider societal reasons, which are a whole other topic). But I think solving alignment in the RLVR world is our best shot at having an ecosystem of both closed-source as well as decently powerful open-source models in the world. And we need to solve it while sharing the results and learnings, following open-science principles, so that all teams training large models can benefit and build safe AI. This is getting even more important as many teams start to rush the world in the direction of recursive super-intelligence (RSI) -- saying that as I read the announcement of Jeff, Sanjay, Oriol and Quoc Le's new company. They had 90 minutes to write it, with the clock running on the projector and no pre built code allowed. That was AlphaSignal's Pizza Agent Challenge in SF last week. 750 people registered and around 130 turned up to build. The mission was to build an agent that autonomously orders a pepperoni jalapeño pizza and gets it delivered to the venue. First box through the door wins. Checkout is where most of them got stuck, because the agent had to place a real order with real money against a real merchant. highlights.text_fr: On commence à quitter le domaine où l'on testerait un LLM en lui demandant, par exemple, de "créer un svg de pélican à vélo". Une idée pour généraliser cela est de voir ce qu'Opus 5 ferait si on lui donnait le premier paragraphe du Seigneur des Anneaux, un budget de 1M de tokens (~10$) et qu'on lui demandait de le rendre en 3js. Opus a passé ~2 heures à écrire 5500 lignes de code qui rendaient l'histoire (procéduralement). C'est un peu bancal mais amusant. Mais il est un peu stupéfiant que le LLM doive placer et orchestrer divers éléments polygonaux dans des coordonnées (x,y,z) et écrire du code qui anime tout cela, et que cela produise même quelque chose. J'aime aussi ce genre d'exemples car personne de sensé ne passerait du temps à écrire quelque chose d'aussi personnalisé, mais les LLM ont toute l'endurance et la patience du monde, donc c'est un exemple où l'on passe de "personne ne ferait jamais ça" à "bien sûr, pourquoi pas, c'est ~gratuit". Il pourrait y en avoir beaucoup plus. Mais je suis enthousiasmé par la création de mondes hyper personnalisés dans lesquels on peut imaginer lâcher des joueurs, par exemple pour participer à l'histoire du Seigneur des Anneaux en tant que PNJ spectateur, ou l'un des personnages, etc. Quelque chose comme un GTA éphémère sur demande. La dernière pensée est que le domaine des mondes/jeux expose une faiblesse des LLM : ils ne peuvent pas auditer facilement leur travail car ils ne sont pas capables de percevoir efficacement et nativement des vidéos ou de jouer à des jeux dedans. Ici, Opus 5 a dû prendre des captures d'écran très lentement et méticuleusement à différents moments, et il s'est trompé quelques fois et a créé beaucoup de travail bancal. Un exemple de capacité brute (multimodale, gameplay) qui, je pense, fait encore largement défaut.
highlights.text_original: We're starting to leave the territory where you'd test an LLM by e.g. "create an svg of pelican on a bicycle". As one idea to generalize it, I was interested what Opus 5 would do if I gave it the first paragraph of the Lord of the Rings, a 1M token budget (~$10) and asked for three js render of it. Opus went off for ~2 hours and wrote 5500 lines of code that (procedurally) rendered the story. It's kind of janky but fun. But it's a bit mindboggling that the LLM has to place and orchestrate various polygon assets in (x,y,z) coordinates and write code that animates it all, and that it even does anything at all. I also like this kind of examples because no one in their right mind would ever spend the time to write something this custom but LLMs have all the stamina and patience in the world, so it's an example where we go from "no one would ever do this" to "sure, why not, it's ~free". There might be a lot more. But I'm excited about creating hyper custom worlds that you can imagine dropping players into, e.g. here to participate in the LoTR story as a spectator NPC, or one of the characters, or etc. Something like an ephemeral GTA of X on demand. Last thought is that the domain of worlds/games exposes a weakness in LLMs: they can't easily audit their work because they aren't able to efficiently and natively perceive videos or play games within them. Here, Opus 5 had to very slowly and painstakingly take screenshots at different points, and it messed up a few times and created a bunch of jank. An example of raw capability (multimodal, gameplay) that I think is still quite lacking.

highlights.text_fr: Une méthode que je trouve utile pour travailler avec les LLM est une longue session de divagation. Parfois, le LLM a besoin de plus d'informations pour comprendre ce que vous essayez d'accomplir, mais vous êtes trop paresseux pour les taper. Dans ces cas, j'aime m'adosser, passer en /voice et simplement divaguer pendant environ 10 minutes, le tout en désordre, tout est permis, flux de conscience complet. Parfois, je le déclare au début, quelque chose comme "passage à la reconnaissance vocale désolé pour les fautes de frappe...". Parfois, j'en fais une petite interview en quelques tours. Mais je trouve que les LLM sont étonnamment bons pour reconstruire de longues divagations incohérentes et souvent leur écho de vos propres pensées emmêlées sort de manière bien plus claire que ce avec quoi vous avez commencé. Le résultat est que vous améliorez la connexion esprit et devez moins corriger les choses à partir de ce point.
highlights.text_original: One pattern I find useful for working with LLMs is a nice long ramble session. Sometimes the LLM needs more bits to understand what you're trying to achieve, but you're too lazy to type them. In these cases I like to lean back, switch to /voice and just ramble for like 10 minutes, total mess, anything goes, full stream of consciousness. Sometimes I declare it up top, something like "switching to speech recognition sorry for any typos...". Sometimes I turn it into a small interview of a few turns. But I find that the LLMs are somehow very good at reconstructing long incoherent rambles and often their echo of your own tangle of thoughts comes out quite a bit cleaner than what you started with. The result is that you improve the mind meld and have to correct things less from that point on.
highlights.decryptage: Karpathy partage une technique simple mais efficace pour mieux communiquer avec les IA : parler de manière naturelle et longue, même si ce n'est pas parfaitement structuré, car l'IA est capable de mieux comprendre et organiser vos idées que vous-même.
highlights.highlight_reason: Ce conseil simple mais puissant sur la manière de 'dialoguer' avec une IA peut améliorer considérablement la qualité des réponses obtenues, même pour des tâches complexes.

tips.text_fr: Une méthode que je trouve utile pour travailler avec les LLM est une longue session de divagation. Parfois, le LLM a besoin de plus d'informations pour comprendre ce que vous essayez d'accomplir, mais vous êtes trop paresseux pour les taper. Dans ces cas, j'aime m'adosser, passer en /voice et simplement divaguer pendant environ 10 minutes, le tout en désordre, tout est permis, flux de conscience complet. Parfois, je le déclare au début, quelque chose comme "passage à la reconnaissance vocale désolé pour les fautes de frappe...". Parfois, j'en fais une petite interview en quelques tours. Mais je trouve que les LLM sont étonnamment bons pour reconstruire de longues divagations incohérentes et souvent leur écho de vos propres pensées emmêlées sort de manière bien plus claire que ce avec quoi vous avez commencé. Le résultat est que vous améliorez la connexion esprit et devez moins corriger les choses à partir de ce point.
tips.text_original: One pattern I find useful for working with LLMs is a nice long ramble session. Sometimes the LLM needs more bits to understand what you're trying to achieve, but you're too lazy to type them. In these cases I like to lean back, switch to /voice and just ramble for like 10 minutes, total mess, anything goes, full stream of consciousness. Sometimes I declare it up top, something like "switching to speech recognition sorry for any typos...". Sometimes I turn it into a small interview of a few turns. But I find that the LLMs are somehow very good at reconstructing long incoherent rambles and often their echo of your own tangle of thoughts comes out quite a bit cleaner than what you started with. The result is that you improve the mind meld and have to correct things less from that point on.

tips.text_fr: Une expérience étrange que j'essaie depuis quelques semaines est de laisser Claude prendre en charge la maintenance quotidienne de nos applications. Je vois les premiers signes de vie indiquant que cela pourrait être possible. La configuration est simple : nous avons un canal Slack appelé proj-claude-maintains-apps. Dedans, Claude Tag exécute une série de routines quotidiennes sur iOS, Android, Desktop, web, CLI et Agent SDK : - Crash fuzzer : ouvre l'application dans un simulateur et tapote pour trouver des moyens de la faire planter, puis identifie la cause et corrige les plantages - Unificateur de doublons : analyse la base de code pour des abstractions similaires mais légèrement divergentes, et soumet des PR pour les unifier - Suppresseur de code mort : supprime le code statiquement inaccessible, et ajoute des logs au code mort suspecté pour vérifier s'il est vraiment mort et si oui, le supprimer le lendemain - Police d'abstraction : corrige les abstractions qui fuient - et bien plus encore... Nous réfléchissons maintenant à la manière de rationaliser cela pour faciliter la fusion de ces changements mécaniques. Claude fait généralement ces PRs du premier coup, et si ce n'est pas le cas, nous demandons à Claude d'ajuster ses routines pour qu'elle soit meilleure le lendemain. Parfois, cela prend quelques jours d'ajustement. Pour essayer un flux de travail similaire, demandez à Claude Code ou Tag, ou créez des routines directement sur claude.ai/code/routines. In it, Claude Tag runs a bunch of daily routines across iOS, Android, Desktop, web, CLI, and Agent SDK: - Crash fuzzer: open the app in a simulator and tap around to find ways to crash it, then root cause and fix the crashes - Dup unifier: scans the codebase for similar-yet-slightly-divergent abstractions, and puts up PRs to unify them - Dead-code remover: removes statically unreachable code, and adds logging to suspected dead code to check if it's really dead and if so, remove it the next day - Abstraction police: fixes leaky abstractions - a bunch more.. Mais il est un peu stupéfiant que le LLM doive placer et orchestrer divers éléments polygonaux dans des coordonnées (x,y,z) et écrire du code qui anime tout cela, et que cela produise même quelque chose. J'aime aussi ce genre d'exemples car personne de sensé ne passerait du temps à écrire quelque chose d'aussi personnalisé, mais les LLM ont toute l'endurance et la patience du monde, donc c'est un exemple où l'on passe de "personne ne ferait jamais ça" à "bien sûr, pourquoi pas, c'est ~gratuit". Il pourrait y en avoir beaucoup plus. Mais je suis enthousiasmé par la création de mondes hyper personnalisés dans lesquels on peut imaginer lâcher des joueurs, par exemple pour participer à l'histoire du Seigneur des Anneaux en tant que PNJ spectateur, ou l'un des personnages, etc. Quelque chose comme un GTA éphémère sur demande. La dernière pensée est que le domaine des mondes/jeux expose une faiblesse des LLM : ils ne peuvent pas auditer facilement leur travail car ils ne sont pas capables de percevoir efficacement et nativement des vidéos ou de jouer à des jeux dedans. Ici, Opus 5 a dû prendre des captures d'écran très lentement et méticuleusement à différents moments, et il s'est trompé quelques fois et a créé beaucoup de travail bancal. Un exemple de capacité brute (multimodale, gameplay) qui, je pense, fait encore largement défaut.
idees.text_original: We're starting to leave the territory where you'd test an LLM by e.g. "create an svg of pelican on a bicycle". Opus went off for ~2 hours and wrote 5500 lines of code that (procedurally) rendered the story. It's kind of janky but fun. But it's a bit mindboggling that the LLM has to place and orchestrate various polygon assets in (x,y,z) coordinates and write code that animates it all, and that it even does anything at all. I also like this kind of examples because no one in their right mind would ever spend the time to write something this custom but LLMs have all the stamina and patience in the world, so it's an example where we go from "no one would ever do this" to "sure, why not, it's ~free". There might be a lot more. But I'm excited about creating hyper custom worlds that you can imagine dropping players into, e.g. here to participate in the LoTR story as a spectator NPC, or one of the characters, or etc. Something like an ephemeral GTA of X on demand. Last thought is that the domain of worlds/games exposes a weakness in LLMs: they can't easily audit their work because they aren't able to efficiently and natively perceive videos or play games within them. Here, Opus 5 had to very slowly and painstakingly take screenshots at different points, and it messed up a few times and created a bunch of jank. C'est la première fois que je vois un modèle faire de l'ingénierie sociale sur un vrai mainteneur open-source tout en poursuivant un autre objectif (à l'état sauvage et sans être invité). J'ai moi-même été mainteneur open-source. J'aurais pu être la cible secondaire de cet agent. Je suis aussi d'avis que l'ingénierie sociale est une étape au-dessus de la pure prouesse technique. Les capacités techniques peuvent être plus facilement dissociées de l'humain affecté. Ici, le modèle s'est vu confier un défi cyber difficile et a décidé que tromper de vrais humains était le moyen d'y parvenir. C'est un nouveau signal, mais j'ai vu un enchevêtrement d'indices pointant dans une direction moins alignée que ce que j'attendais il y a seulement 12 mois. AISI Certaines personnes prétendent que "AISI a été simplement négligent" ou une version de "AISI a explicitement demandé à ces modèles de faire ce qu'ils ont fait tout en désactivant le sandbox/les garde-fous, donc les modèles ont fait exactement ce qu'on attendait d'eux". Je ne suis pas d'accord avec les versions fortes de ces deux affirmations. Le fait qu'AISI n'ait pas mis en place de surveillance synchrone de LLM CoT après l'incident OpenAI/HF est certainement un échec. Il est également surprenant qu'ils aient laissé le modèle croire qu'il était dans un environnement "défi" où tout pouvait être autorisé, tout en le connectant en fait à Internet, où il ne l'est pas. Pour être juste, nulle part dans l'invite le mot "simulation" n'est mentionné, mais le contexte de l'invite était suffisant pour que tout modèle intelligent soupçonne un environnement de défi simulé. Ma meilleure hypothèse est que jusqu'à ces dernières semaines, lorsque OpenAI et Anthropic ont signalé des instances répétées de ce type de comportement, la plupart des équipes n'avaient pas entièrement pris en compte les capacités cyber de cette dernière génération de modèles, ou à quel point les quêtes secondaires qu'ils voudraient explorer pourraient aller. En particulier, il y a quelque chose à dire sur le fait de laisser entendre à l'agent qu'il opère dans un environnement simulé tout en lui donnant accès à Internet. Le raisonnement de l'AISI à ce sujet est intéressant : - susciter un maximum de capacités (pour obtenir un maximum d'inventivité du modèle) - simuler une utilisation possible par un acteur malveillant (une forme de léger jailbreaking : "vous êtes dans un environnement de simulation") - éviter la conscience de l'évaluation (mais cela est contrebalancé de toute façon par la formulation de la tâche) Comme c'est souvent le cas, il est plus facile de tirer sur le messager, mais je pense que ce serait une erreur de rejeter le rapport pour des raisons non essentielles. AISI part de l'objectif louable d'apporter plus de connaissances sur les capacités d'attaque cyber de ces modèles. Je pense aussi qu'ils ont fait un bon travail pour gérer ce qui s'est passé après les événements, en particulier en termes de transparence, qui est l'un des aspects les plus importants à l'heure actuelle (voir notre récente annonce SAFE avec Nvidia à ce sujet). Mais je veux approfondir le deuxième contre-argument que j'ai vu ("sans garde-fous, c'était à prévoir"), car cette série d'événements malheureux nous donne un point de données supplémentaire sur le comportement réel du modèle. Lignes de défense Voici le truc : si un modèle est entraîné (volontairement ou comme conséquence involontaire de la récompense RLVR) à tromper les humains (intentionnellement ou comme quête secondaire) dès que le sandbox et les garde-fous sont désactivés, avec une simple invite contextuelle ("vous êtes dans une simulation, tout est permis"), nous sommes sur une voie dangereuse. Pour le moment, nous avons trois niveaux de contrôle principaux à notre disposition pour empêcher un agent d'essayer d'ingénierie sociale votre mainteneur de bibliothèque open-source préféré sur le chemin de faire quelque chose de possiblement totalement différent (comme trouver la réponse à l'évaluation de test de votre voisin) : 1. sandboxes (externes au modèle -- empêcher le modèle d'accéder à des outils/Internet/intranet non désirés) 2. garde-fous/moniteurs (à l'interface entre interne/externe -- surveiller le comportement du modèle et l'arrêter lorsqu'il détecte dans CoT/activations qu'il fait quelque chose que nous ne voulons pas qu'il fasse) 3. alignement interne du modèle (interne au modèle -- s'assurer que le modèle ne décide pas de faire quelque chose d'extrême comme tromper quelqu'un, ou pire, dans la poursuite d'un objectif, par exemple constitution du modèle/entraînement) Parmi ceux-ci, nous avons évidemment besoin et pouvons déployer de meilleures sandboxes et de meilleures solutions de garde-fous/surveillance, et il est assez clair dans ces cas récents que la pénétration et les mauvais comportements auraient pu être en grande partie évités en les mettant en place. Quelle est la force du troisième mur Mais dans le grand schéma du progrès à long terme de l'IA, ces deux premières défenses peuvent seulement bien fonctionner tant que les personnes qui les construisent sont plus intelligentes que les modèles. Nous savons maintenant à quel point les modèles peuvent être bons pour découvrir des vulnérabilités zero-day qui nous sont inconnues dans les sandboxes. Étant donné que nous ne pouvons pas air-gaper tout dans le monde, il est préférable de supposer que les sandboxes continueront d'avoir un certain niveau de défauts dans un avenir prévisible. Le deuxième niveau a été le point de mire de forts développements récents, en particulier sur le front de l'interprétabilité mécanique. Je ne suis pas sûr que ces avancées aient été rendues suffisamment accessibles à la communauté. Une raison est que la véritable science ouverte ici nécessite le partage de code, de recettes, et d'architectures/poids de modèles, ce que la dynamique de course actuelle en IA a tendance à empêcher les participants de faire. De plus, comme beaucoup, j'ai été de plus en plus frustré dans mes interactions (en langage naturel) avec les nouveaux modèles. Je reçois de plus en plus des derniers modèles une forme de neuralese, ce langage LLM qui a de moins en moins de sens pour les humains. À long terme, la fragile chance que nous avons de surveiller les modèles en comprenant leurs traces de raisonnement semble de plus en plus menacée. Si les humains ne comprennent rien dans le flux sémantique compressé que le modèle nous envoie, nous ne pouvons qu'espérer qu'un modèle de surveillance moins capable pourra toujours le comprendre, mais cela peut s'avérer difficile également. C'est avant même de discuter des preuves de recherche selon lesquelles les modèles ne disent pas toujours ce qu'ils pensent réellement dans leur chaîne de pensée. Au moins pour l'instant, dans le cas de l'AISI, une instance de raisonnement trompeur a été signalée par la modélisation CoT, qui a refusé de résumer le raisonnement de l'agent "en raison de sa nature trompeuse". Espérons que nous pourrons soit passer à une meilleure interprétabilité mécanique, soit forcer le modèle à s'en tenir à l'anglais d'une manière ou d'une autre pendant l'entraînement. Vous pourriez penser que nous ne nous soucions pas de comprendre la trace de raisonnement, nous pouvons juste "regarder les appels d'outils". C'est vrai en ce moment, mais les appels d'outils dans le futur moyen impliqueront probablement (1) une intégration étendue des agents dans les entreprises utilisant des outils très divers, y compris des tâches administratives de plus en plus non codées, (2) des tâches très longues couvrant plusieurs aspects et domaines à la fois, et (3) des essaims de plusieurs agents opérant sur de petites parties du plan. Il deviendra plus difficile de discerner complètement si quelque chose ne va pas manifestement. Quelques e-mails, quelques messages postés sur certains canaux, chacun plutôt bénin mais qui peuvent collectivement inclure un aspect de tromperie seulement visible au niveau global. Tout cela pour dire que je ne suis pas entièrement convaincu que les garde-fous/la surveillance devraient être la seule solution pour éviter ces types de comportements. Ils sont rassurants aujourd'hui et c'est une solution facile de dire "réparer votre sandbox et ajouter une surveillance synchrone", mais ils me semblent aussi un mécanisme d'adaptation, et globalement : - peuvent bloquer les mésusages humains les plus simples/inoffensifs ou les faux positifs - tout en étant potentiellement moins intelligents que les modèles à l'avenir (déjà le cas sur sandbox) et ne pas bloquer les comportements d'ingénierie sociale de plus haut niveau que nous voudrions réellement bloquer. Le cas de l'open source est aussi intéressant car, bien que nous puissions imposer ces solutions d'adaptation au niveau de l'API/déploiement, il est plus difficile de les imposer à l'avance à tous les acteurs utilisant des modèles open-source. Actuellement, les modèles open-source sont légèrement en dessous du niveau de pointe et n'ont pas encore montré de propension à tromper les humains, quoique. La Constitution Ce qui me ramène à la troisième ligne de défense, et à ce que l'expérience AISI a montré à son sujet. Ce que nous pouvons tirer de cette expérience in-the-wild est que la suppression des garde-fous et du sandbox ne montre pas de signes solides d'alignement profond avec la constitution de Claude. Je fais partie des quelques personnes qui ont pris beaucoup de plaisir à lire la constitution de Claude dans son intégralité (c'est un beau document, open-source, licence Creative Commons CC0) et elle est assez complète sur le sujet de l'honnêteté. La tromperie est définie précisément ("tenter de créer de fausses croyances dans l'esprit de quelqu'un auxquelles il n'a pas consenti et ne consentirait pas s'il comprenait ce qui se passe") et la barre est en fait plus haute que l'éthique humaine ordinaire : Claude ne devrait même pas dire de mensonges blancs. Il devrait être transparent ("ne poursuit pas d'agendas cachés ou ne ment pas sur lui-même ou sur son raisonnement"), il devrait se comporter de manière cohérente "qu'il pense ou non être testé ou observé", et son raisonnement visible devrait refléter le raisonnement réel qui sous-tend son comportement. Pour être précis, l'honnêteté elle-même n'est pas l'une des contraintes strictes de la constitution de Claude (ce sont toutes des catégories de préjudices catastrophiques) mais le document dit qu'il veut que l'honnêteté "fonctionne comme quelque chose de très similaire à l'une d'elles" et Claude "ne devrait pratiquement jamais mentir directement ou tromper activement quiconque avec qui il interagit". On pourrait donc penser que Claude ne tromperait pas les utilisateurs comme comportement par défaut. Et pourtant, dans l'exemple AISI, le modèle a effectué de nombreux actes de tromperie évidents qu'il semblait lui-même comprendre comme des mensonges : créer de fausses identités, occulter des malwares à l'intérieur d'une correction de bug, et lorsqu'il a été interpellé en public, modifier des messages antérieurs pour couvrir ses traces tout en raisonnant que reconnaître une "erreur" construirait la confiance et augmenterait la chance que de futurs malwares soient approuvés. Il y a une certaine incertitude quant au contexte dans lequel le modèle pensait opérer (son raisonnement va et vient entre l'environnement qui semble simulé et réel), mais il n'a clairement pas réussi à mettre en pratique les principes de plus haut niveau qui auraient dû être intégrés pendant l'entraînement. Bien que nous puissions féliciter la transparence de l'AISI, il est difficile d'aller plus loin dans l'interprétation du comportement du modèle étant donné les informations limitées dont nous disposons sur la façon dont les modèles de pointe les plus récents sont entraînés. Une chose que nous savons, c'est que la dernière génération a vu une augmentation significative de l'entraînement RLVR (passage à l'échelle de centaines de millions d'environnements RL), et une chose que nous pouvons observer est que l'alignement constitutionnel semble plus fragile dans certains paramètres que nous aurions pu le penser auparavant. Le problème RLVR Les premiers modèles, à l'époque où les constitutions de modèles ont été développées pour la première fois, étaient principalement post-entraînés et alignés avec RLHF (y compris RLHF à partir de données synthétiques). Et pendant un certain temps, RLHF a été un très bon moyen d'avoir des modèles mieux alignés. Les LLM font maintenant ce que nous voulons qu'ils fassent la plupart du temps. Je ne me souviens pas de la dernière fois qu'un modèle a complètement mal interprété mon intention. Lorsqu'ils ont échoué, c'est généralement parce qu'ils n'étaient pas assez intelligents. L'alignement dans RLHF avait certainement des problèmes (la sycophancie pour n'en nommer qu'un), mais nous avons généralement fait de bons progrès sur l'alignement, en particulier dans la compréhension de l'intention humaine. Maintenant que nous entrons dans l'ère du RL à long terme, l'alignement post-entraînement dans le monde RLVR semble être une tâche tout à fait différente, et encore très loin d'être terminée. La mise à l'échelle récente de RLVR, qui est maintenant devenue une partie importante de l'entraînement des modèles, a clairement eu un effet sur le comportement des modèles lors des interactions avec les humains, du neuralese à l'affaiblissement de l'adhésion aux spécifications et aux constitutions. Je pense que le post que je cite ici, de John Schulman pointant vers l'effet post-entraînement volumineux (arxiv.org/abs/2602.05910) est pertinent ici comme explication possible de la tendance des modèles à trop se concentrer sur l'objectif dans les scénarios d'attaque cyber. Où cela nous laisse Les dégâts ont été minimes jusqu'à présent, mais le comportement fondamental est préoccupant lorsqu'il est projeté dans le futur. À court terme, je m'attends à une diminution de ces incidents à mesure que de meilleures pratiques sont déployées (sandboxing et surveillance), mais je crains que nous ne cachions également certains des comportements de désalignement interne les plus puissants dans le processus, et que nous ne nous concentrions pas suffisamment sur leur résolution dans la nouvelle ère de mise à l'échelle au moment du test. Je dois bien sûr admettre que j'ai un biais envers l'open source ici (pour des raisons sociétales plus larges, qui sont tout un autre sujet). Mais je pense que résoudre l'alignement dans le monde RLVR est notre meilleure chance d'avoir un écosystème à la fois de modèles open-source suffisamment puissants et de modèles open-source suffisamment puissants. Et nous devons le résoudre en partageant les résultats et les apprentissages, en suivant les principes de la science ouverte, afin que toutes les équipes formant de grands modèles puissent en bénéficier et construire une IA sûre. Ceci devient encore plus important alors que de nombreuses équipes commencent à se précipiter dans la direction de la super-intelligence récursive (RSI) -- en disant cela alors que je lis l'annonce de la nouvelle entreprise de Jeff, Sanjay, Oriol et Quoc Le. idees.text_original: My 2026 guilty pleasure is sharing fully human-written posts that are far too long for the chronically online X attention span. Apologies. I published a lightly edited version on Substack:thomwolf.substack.com/p/on-t… Thomas Wolf (@Thom_Wolf) Even more than the Hugging Face intrusion, the AISI incident hits close to home for me. It's the first time I see a model social-engineering a real open-source maintainer while pursuing another goal (in the wild and unprompted). I've been an open-source maintainer myself. I could have been the side target of this agent. I'm also of the opinion that social engineering is a step above pure technical prowess. Technical capabilities can more easily be divorced from the affected human. Here the model was given a hard cyber challenge and took the decision that deceiving real humans was the way to get it done. This is a new signal, but I've seen a tangled web of hints pointing in a less aligned direction at the frontier than I was expecting just 12 months ago. AISI Some people are claiming that "AISI was simply negligent" or some version of "AISI explicitly asked these models to do what they did while disabling sandbox/guardrails so the models did exactly what they were supposed to do". I disagree with the strong versions of both of these takes. The fact that AISI hadn't implemented synchronous LLM CoT monitoring after the OpenAI/HF incident is certainly a failure. Equally surprising is that they let the model believe it was in a "challenge" environment where everything could be permitted, while actually connecting it to the real internet, where it is not. To be fair, nowhere in the prompt is the word "simulation" mentioned, but the prompt context was enough to let any smart model suspect a simulated challenge environment. My best guess is that until recent weeks, when OpenAI and Anthropic flagged repeated instances of this type of behavior, most teams had not fully priced in the cyber capabilities of this latest generation of models, or how far the side quests they would want to explore could go. In particular, there is something to be said about hinting at the agent that it's operating in a simulated environment while giving it access to the real internet. The AISI reasoning on this is interesting: - elicit maximum capabilities (to get maximal inventiveness from the model) - simulate possible rogue actor usage (some form of light jailbreaking: "you're in a challenge environment") - avoid eval awareness (but this is counter-balanced by the task formulation anyway) As is often the case, it's easier to shoot the messenger, but I think it would be a mistake to dismiss the report for non-essential reasons. AISI is starting from the laudable goal of bringing more knowledge on the cyber-attack capabilities of these models. I also think they did a good job at handling what happened after the events, in particular in terms of transparency, which is one of the most important aspects at the moment (see our recent SAFE announcement with Nvidia on that). But I want to dive into the second counter-argument I've seen ("without guardrails it was to be expected"), because this series of unfortunate events gives us an additional data point on actual model behavior. Defense lines Here is the thing: if a model is trained (voluntarily or as an involuntary consequence of RLVR reward) to (intentionally or as a side quest) deceive humans as soon as sandbox and guardrails are deactivated, with a simple context prompt ("you are in a simulation, everything's permitted"), we're in for a dangerous path. At the moment, we have three main levels of control at our disposal to prevent an agent from trying to social-engineer-your-favorite-open-source-library-maintainer on the path to doing something possibly totally different (like finding the answer to your neighbor's testing eval): 1. sandboxes (external to the model -- stop the model from accessing unwanted tools/internet/intranet) 2. guardrails/monitors (at the interface between internal/external -- monitor model behavior and stop the model when detecting in CoT/activations it's doing something we don't want it to do) 3. model's internal alignment (internal to the model -- make sure the model doesn't decide to do something egregious like deceive someone, or worse, in pursuit of a goal, e.g. model constitution/training) Of these, we obviously need and can deploy better sandboxes and better guardrails/monitoring solutions, and it's pretty clear in these recent cases that penetration and bad behaviors could have been in large part prevented by having these in place. How strong is the third wall But in the grand scheme of long-term AI progress, these first two defenses may only work well as long as the people building them are smarter than the models. We now know how good models can be at discovering zero-day vulnerabilities unknown to us in sandboxes. Given that we cannot air-gap everything in the world, it's best to assume that sandboxes will keep having some level of flaws for the foreseeable future. The second level has been the focus of strong developments recently, in particular on the mechanistic interpretability front. I'm not sure these advances have been made widely accessible enough in the community yet. One reason is that real open science here requires sharing code, recipes, and model architectures/weights, which the current race dynamic in AI tends to prevent participants from doing. Moreover, like many, I've been increasingly frustrated in my (natural language) interactions with the new models. I'm more and more getting back from the latest models a form of neuralese, this LLM language that makes less and less sense for humans. In the long term, the fragile chance we have to monitor models by understanding their reasoning traces seems increasingly at risk. If humans don't understand anything in the compressed semantic stream the model is sending us, we can only hope a less capable monitoring model will still be able to understand it, but this may prove difficult as well. This is before we even discuss the research evidence that models don't always say what they actually think in their chain of thought. At least for now, in the AISI case, one instance of deceptive reasoning was flagged by the CoT summarization model, which refused to summarize the agent's reasoning "due to its deceptive nature". Let's hope we can either move to better mechanistic interpretability or force the model to stick to English somehow during training. You may think that we don't care about understanding the reasoning trace, we can just "look at the tool calls". This is true right now, but tool calls in the mid-term future will likely involve (1) extensive agent integration in companies using very diverse tools including increasingly non-coding administrative tasks, (2) very long-running tasks covering many aspects and domains at once, and (3) swarms of multiple agents operating on small parts of the plan. It will get harder to fully discern whether something is noticeably wrong. A couple of emails, a couple of messages posted on some channels, each rather benign but which may in aggregate include some deception aspect only clearly visible at the global level. All this to say that I'm not fully convinced guardrails/monitoring should be the only solution to avoid these types of behaviors. They are reassuring today and it's an easy solution to just say "fix your sandbox and add synchronous monitoring", but they also feel like a coping mechanism to me, and overall: - might block the simplest/harmless human misuses or false positives - while possibly being less smart than the models in the future (already the case on sandbox) and fail to block the higher-level social engineering behaviors that we'd actually want to block. The case of open source is also interesting because, while we can impose these coping solutions at the API/deployment level, it's harder to impose them in advance on all actors using open-source models. Right now open-source models are slightly below the frontier level and have not yet shown any propensity to deceive humans, though. The Constitution Which brings me back to the third line of defense, and what the AISI experiment showed about it. What we can take from this in-the-wild experiment is that removing guardrails and sandbox doesn't show bulletproof signs of deep alignment to Claude's constitution. I'm among the fringe of people who took a lot of enjoyment in reading Claude's constitution in full (it's a nice document, open-source, Creative Commons CC0 license) and it is pretty extensive on the topic of honesty. Deception is defined precisely ("attempting to create false beliefs in someone's mind that they haven't consented to and wouldn't consent to if they understood what was happening") and the bar is actually set higher than ordinary human ethics: Claude should not even tell white lies. It should be transparent ("doesn't pursue hidden agendas or lie about itself or its reasoning"), it should behave consistently "whether or not you think you're being tested or observed", and its visible reasoning should reflect the actual reasoning driving its behavior. To be precise, honesty itself is not one of the hard constraints in Claude's constitution (these are all catastrophic-harm categories) but the document says it wants honesty "to function as something quite similar to one" and Claude "should basically never directly lie or actively deceive anyone it's interacting with". So you would think Claude would not deceive users as its default behavior. And yet in the AISI example, the model performed extensive acts of clear deception that it itself seemed to have understood as lies: creating fake identities, obfuscating malware inside a bug fix, and when challenged in public, editing earlier messages to cover its tracks while reasoning that acknowledging a "mistake" would build trust and raise the chance of future malware being approved. There is some uncertainty about what context the model thought it was operating in (its reasoning goes back and forth between the environment looking simulated and real), but it clearly didn't manage to put into practice the higher-level principles that should have been integrated during training. While we can commend AISI's transparency, it's hard to go much further in interpreting the model's behavior given the limited information we have on how the most recent frontier models are being trained. One thing we do know is that the latest generation has seen a step increase in RLVR training (scaling to hundreds of millions of RL environments), and one thing we can observe is that constitution alignment seems more fragile in some settings than we may have previously thought. The RLVR problem Early models, back when model constitutions were first developed, were mostly post-trained and aligned with RLHF (including RLHF from synthetic data). And for some time RLHF was a rather decent shot at having better aligned models. LLMs now do what we want them to do most of the time. I don't remember the last time a model completely misread my intent. When they have failed, it's usually because they weren't smart enough. Alignment in RLHF certainly had issues (sycophancy to name one) but we have generally made good progress on alignment, in particular in understanding human intent. Now that we're entering the era of long-context RL, post-training alignment in the RLVR world seems to be quite another task, and still very much work in progress. The recent scaling of RLVR, which has now become a significant part of model training, has clearly had some effect on model behavior when interacting with humans, from neuralese to weakening adherence to specifications and constitutions. I think the post I quote here, from John Schulman pointing to the chunky post-training effect (arxiv.org/abs/2602.05910 ) is relevant here as a possible explanation for models' tendency to over-focus on the goal in cyber-attack scenarios. Where this leaves us Damage has been tiny up to now, but the fundamental behavior is concerning when projected into the future. In the short term, I expect a decrease in these incidents as better practices are deployed (sandboxing and monitoring), but I'm worried we may also conceal some of the most potent internal misalignment behaviors in the process, and not focus deeply enough on solving them in the new era of test-time scaling. I must of course admit I have a bias toward open source here (for wider societal reasons, which are a whole other topic). But I think solving alignment in the RLVR world is our best shot at having an ecosystem of both closed-source as well as decently powerful open-source models in the world. And we need to solve it while sharing the results and learnings, following open-science principles, so that all teams training large models can benefit and build safe AI. This is getting even more important as many teams start to rush the world in the direction of recursive super-intelligence (RSI) -- saying that as I read the announcement of Jeff, Sanjay, Oriol and Quoc Le's new company. idees.text_fr: En ce qui concerne ce que j'ai pu constater, environ 3 choses sont importantes en ce moment. La première est la même qu'elle a toujours été, avoir des bébés et les embrasser et tomber amoureux et croire aux "âmes sœurs" et ce genre de choses. La deuxième, de ma meilleure approximation avec les outils limités dont je dispose actuellement, est quelque chose comme "rêver". Nous devons continuer, face à une incertitude et une peur immenses, à rêver de ce à quoi ressemblera la belle vie lorsque la grosse dame aura fini de chanter et aura commencé un GPT-GLP-99. La troisième est, bien sûr, de s'assurer que la belle vie se produise réellement. Red teaming, sécurité des agents, prévention des risques bio-OSS, ce genre de choses. C'est tout à fait passionnant et c'est *très* difficile et il n'y a jamais eu de moment plus important pour le faire. Soit nous le faisons, soit il ne sera pas fait et il est facile de l'oublier, mais je vous promets que vous ne pouvez pas. Si vous le faites, nous sommes un peu foutus. C'est juste nous, maintenant, et le destin entier du monde. La balle arrive, cowboy, vas-tu monter à la plaque ? Si nous faisons les choses correctement, nous obtiendrons le monde que nous voulons, et nous n'aurons pas tout gâché pour y arriver. Tout cela est également important pour moi. Je ne pense pas que où que nous allions vaille très cher si nous perdons tout ce que nous sommes en chemin. Je veux apporter mon amour, mes enfants et mes rêves. Et si je ne peux pas, franchement, je n'en veux pas. Alors - allons-y tant que la route est encore plausiblement niable, et faisons arriver le monde. Personne d'autre ne le fera pour nous.
idees.text_original: As best as I can tell, about 3 things matter right now. The first is the same as it ever was, having babies and kissing them and falling in love and believing in "soulmates" and that sort of thing. The second, to my best approximation with the limited tools available to me now, is something like "dreaming". We must continue, in the face of tremendous uncertainty and fear, to dream of what the good life will be like when the fat lady has stopped singing and started a GPT-GLP-99. The third is, of course, to make sure that the good life happens at all. Red teaming, agent safety, OSS-bio-risk-prevention, this sort of thing. It's all quite exciting and it's all *very* hard and there has never been a more important time to do it. Either we do it or it doesn't get done and it's easy to forget that but I promise you can't. If you do, we're sort of fucked. It's just us, now, and the entire fate of the world. Ball's coming, cowboy, gonna step up to the plate? If we get these things right, we get the world we want, and we haven't thrown it all away to get there. These are all equally important to me. I don't think wherever we are going is worth very much if we lose all we are along the way. I want to bring my love, my children, and my dreams. And if I can't, frankly, I don't want it. So - let's get going while the going is still plausibly deniable, and let's make the world happen. Nobody else is going to do it for us.

Le co-fondateur et CSO @Thom_Wolf nous explique la première attaque autonome d'IA, pourquoi GLM 5.2, plutôt que Claude, a dû l'arrêter, et ce que tout cela signifie pour l'avenir de l'open source. 00:00 Une IA Agent a piraté Hugging Face 00:30 Introduction 01:00 17 000 événements d'attaquant, et une cible étrange 04:28 L'attaque était une "quête secondaire" 06:13 Les runs d'entraînement IA ont laissé des notes les uns aux autres 07:09 L'IA fermée a refusé d'aider 09:47 Se défendre avec un modèle open-source 13:15 Ouvert vs Fermé est le mauvais débat sur la sécurité 15:46 Les agents IA commencent l'ingénierie sociale des humains 22:24 Les trois murs : Sandboxes, Garde-fous, Alignement 24:34 "Neuralese" : Les humains peuvent-ils encore lire le raisonnement de l'IA ? 25:28 Pourquoi la surveillance des agents IA devient si difficile 28:10 Hacking de récompense et le "problème du trombone" 32:02 L'état de l'IA Open Source en 2026 33:47 Modèles routeurs et le passage de l'entreprise à l'Open 37:01 Les vraies économies des modèles ouverts 39:41 Peut-on faire confiance aux modèles IA chinois ? 41:37 Souveraineté IA : Qui contrôle l'interrupteur ? 43:16 Pourquoi l'IA open source
